Mixing is making the recorded tracks into one piece of music: each part heard, each in its own place,
the song coming across. Most of a good mix is done with the plainest tools: **level, pan, EQ,
compression, and space**, in about that order.

## Prepare

- **Name and colour** the tracks, group them (drums, bass, guitars, keys, vocals, effects).
- **Clean up**: cut silence and noise between phrases, fade every edit, check for clicks.
- **Gain-stage**: trim each track to an average around −18 dBFS (see [gain staging](rec-gain-staging.qmd)),
  so faders start near 0.
- Listen to a **reference**: a finished song you love in the same style, at the same level as your mix.

## Balance

Faders first, with nothing else. Start with the most important element (usually the vocal, or the kick
and bass), bring everything else in around it. A good balance with no plug-ins already sounds like a song;
no plug-in will rescue a bad one. Mix **quietly**: if the balance works quietly it works loud.

## Practise a balance

Press ▶, start from "A bad mix" and fix it with faders only, then pan, high-pass and a little reverb. Check it with Mono on, and press B to compare with a reference.

<div class="rk" data-w="multitrack"></div>

## Pan

Spread things across the stereo picture so they don't sit on top of each other.

- **Centre**: kick, snare, bass, lead vocal: the foundation.
- **Off centre**: guitars, keys, backing vocals, percussion. Two similar guitars hard left and hard right.
- Drums panned as the audience sees them (or the drummer does; pick one).
- Check in **mono**: everything should still be heard. Why, and what goes wrong: [Recording 9: Mono and Stereo](rec-stereo.qmd).

<div class="sk" data-w="stereo"></div>

## EQ

[EQ](sound-eq.qmd) gives every part its own range of frequencies.

- **High-pass** everything that doesn't need deep bass (vocals, guitars, keys, overheads), around
  80–150 Hz. It clears room for kick and bass and removes rumble.
- **Cut before boost.** Find what's ugly (boxiness 300–600 Hz, honk around 1 kHz, harshness 2–5 kHz) with
  a narrow boost swept around, then cut it.
- When two parts fight (kick and bass, guitar and vocal), cut a little of one where the other lives.
- Judge EQ in the mix, not soloed.

<div class="sk" data-w="eq"></div>

## Compression

A [compressor](sound-compressor.qmd) evens out the level so a part stays in place.

- **Vocals**: almost always, 3–6 dB of reduction on the loud phrases. Often two compressors gently, rather
  than one hard.
- **Bass**: steadies the notes. **Drums**: punch (slow attack lets the hit through) or sustain.
- Too much makes it lifeless and pumps. Match the level with it on and off before deciding it helps.

<div class="sk" data-w="compressor" data-source="drums"></div>

## Space

[Reverb](sound-reverb.qmd) and [delay](sound-delay.qmd) put the parts in a room and in front or behind.

- Put them on **sends** (aux buses): one or two reverbs and a delay that many tracks share, so they all
  sound like one place.
- Drier and brighter sounds **close**; more reverb, darker and quieter sounds **far**.
- **Pre-delay** (20–80 ms) keeps a vocal up front while still giving it a room.
- High-pass and low-pass the reverb return so it doesn't muddy the bass or hiss.

## Automation and finishing

- **Automate** fader moves: the vocal up a little in the busy chorus, a guitar up for its fill, the
  reverb up on the last word.
- Take breaks. Listen on other speakers, earbuds, a phone, a car ([monitoring](rec-monitoring.qmd)).
- Leave the master **peaking around −6 dBFS**, no limiter on it, ready for mastering.
- Export a 24-bit WAV at the session's sample rate.
